state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are walking along a path in a park. You start at -12 and walk 10 steps to the right (adding 10). Then, you turn around and walk back 5 steps to the left. Where would you end up? Let's use this real-world scenario to help us find the value of \( b \).

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I start at -12 and walk 10 steps to the right, I think I would end up at -2. But then if I walk back 5 steps to the left, wouldn't I just go to -7? I'm still confused about how that relates to \( b \) though. Does \( b \) mean where I end up after all the steps?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are playing a game where you move along a path. Starting at -12, you move 10 spaces to the right, landing at -2. Then, you move back 5 spaces to the left, ending up at -7. So, \( b \) represents where you end up after all the steps. Can you see how the value of \( b \) is related to the movements along the number line in this game scenario?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get it a bit better now! So, \( b \) is where I end up after moving from -12 to -2 and then back to -7. But I'm still not sure how to find \( b \) if I don't have the steps written out like in the game. Do I just need to remember to add and subtract the numbers?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher never addresses the core misconception that the student thinks arrows start at zero (leading to answer -7), instead providing analogies that accidentally confirm the student's incorrect answer, and by Turn 4 the student still doesn't understand what b represents or how to find it.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds the abstract number line problem in concrete real-world analogies (walking in a park, playing a movement game), making this a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
